stem: Consumer surplus is the difference between

options.content: what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
options.rationale: Correct: the gain from buying at a price below one's valuation.

options.content: what producers receive and the minimum they would accept
options.rationale: That is producer surplus.

options.content: total revenue and total cost
options.rationale: That is profit.

options.content: the equilibrium price and the maximum price
options.rationale: A price control is not part of the definition.

explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay.

stem: On a diagram, producer surplus is the area

options.content: above the supply curve and below the price
options.rationale: Correct: price received less the minimum acceptable price.

options.content: below the demand curve and above the price
options.rationale: That is consumer surplus.

options.content: below the supply curve and above the axis
options.rationale: That is the cost of production.

options.content: between the demand and supply curves beyond equilibrium
options.rationale: That area is the deadweight loss from over-production.

explanation: Producer surplus lies above the supply curve and below the price line, up to the quantity sold.

stem: A rise in the price of a good, with demand unchanged and supply shifting left, will

options.content: increase consumer surplus
options.rationale: A higher price reduces the gap between willingness to pay and price.

options.content: reduce consumer surplus
options.rationale: Correct: consumers pay more and buy less.

options.content: leave consumer surplus unchanged
options.rationale: The area above the price line shrinks.

options.content: increase total surplus
options.rationale: Total surplus falls when supply falls.

explanation: A higher price and a lower quantity reduce consumer surplus.

stem: Which change increases both consumer surplus and producer surplus in a market?

options.content: A fall in demand
options.rationale: Both fall.

options.content: A rise in costs of production
options.rationale: Both fall.

options.content: A rise in demand
options.rationale: Correct: both triangles get larger.

options.content: A maximum price below equilibrium
options.rationale: Producer surplus falls.

explanation: A rise in demand raises the equilibrium price and quantity: producers gain from the higher price, and the demand curve is higher so consumer surplus also rises.

stem: Demand is P = 12 − 0.05Q and the market price is US\$7, so that 100 units are bought. Consumer surplus is

options.rationale: This forgets to halve the triangle.
This is price times quantity (expenditure).
Correct: ½ × 5 × 100.
This is 12 × 100, the area of a rectangle.

explanation: The demand curve meets the price axis at US\$12. Consumer surplus = ½ × (12 − 7) × 100 = US\$250.
hints: Consumer surplus is a triangle between the demand curve and the price.

stem: A maximum price is set below equilibrium. Total surplus falls because

options.content: consumers pay a higher price than before the control
options.rationale: The price is lower under a maximum price.

options.content: producers earn a higher price than at equilibrium
options.rationale: Producers receive less.

options.content: demand falls
options.rationale: The control does not change demand.

options.content: mutually beneficial trades no longer take place
options.rationale: Correct: lost mutually beneficial trades.

explanation: Some units that were worth more to buyers than they cost to produce are no longer traded: a deadweight loss.
hints: Who loses the trades that no longer take place?

stem: A price rise from a cost increase reduces consumer surplus more when demand is

options.content: elastic, because they stop buying at the higher price
options.rationale: Elastic demand means they switch away, so the loss in surplus is smaller.

options.content: inelastic, because they still buy most units at the higher price
options.rationale: Correct: they pay more on the units they cannot give up.

options.content: unitary elastic, because total revenue is unchanged by price
options.rationale: Unitary elasticity has no special effect on surplus here.

options.content: perfectly elastic, because price is unchanged
options.rationale: Consumer surplus is zero with perfectly elastic demand.

explanation: With inelastic demand consumers keep buying at the higher price and so pay more on every unit; the lost surplus is larger.
hints: Compare the steepness of the curves.

stem: Which is a limitation of using consumer surplus to judge a policy?

options.content: It can only be measured for luxuries and not for essentials
options.rationale: It can be measured for any good.

options.content: It is the same as profit earned by a firm
options.rationale: Surplus and profit are different concepts.

options.content: It cannot be shown on a diagram of demand and supply
options.rationale: It is shown as an area.

options.content: It treats a dollar of surplus the same whoever receives it
options.rationale: Correct: it ignores distribution.

explanation: Willingness to pay depends on income, so surplus ignores who gains and loses and the value of fairness.
hints: Willingness to pay depends on income.

stem: A market has demand P = 12 − 0.05Q and supply P = 2 + 0.05Q (P in US\$, Q in units). Calculate consumer surplus at the equilibrium.
explanation: Equilibrium: Q = 100, P = US\$7. Consumer surplus = ½ × (12 − 7) × 100 = US\$250. Forgetting to halve gives 500.
workedSolution: 1. Equilibrium: Q = 100, P = US\$7. Consumer surplus = ½ × (12 − 7) × 100 = US\$250. Forgetting to halve gives 500.

stem: In the same market, a rise in costs shifts supply to P = 4 + 0.05Q. Calculate consumer surplus at the new equilibrium.
explanation: New equilibrium: 12 − 0.05Q = 4 + 0.05Q, so Q = 80 and P = US\$8. Consumer surplus = ½ × (12 − 8) × 80 = US\$160, down from US\$250.
workedSolution: 1. New equilibrium: 12 − 0.05Q = 4 + 0.05Q, so Q = 80 and P = US\$8. Consumer surplus = ½ × (12 − 8) × 80 = US\$160, down from US\$250.

stem: A maximum price of US\$5 is set in the market with demand P = 12 − 0.05Q and supply P = 2 + 0.05Q. Calculate producer surplus after the control.
explanation: At US\$5 only Q = (5 − 2) ÷ 0.05 = 60 units are supplied. Producer surplus = ½ × (5 − 2) × 60 = US\$90, down from US\$250.
workedSolution: 1. At US\$5 only Q = (5 − 2) ÷ 0.05 = 60 units are supplied. Producer surplus = ½ × (5 − 2) × 60 = US\$90, down from US\$250.
hints: Only the quantity supplied is traded at the maximum price.

stem: In the same market with a maximum price of US\$5, 60 units are traded instead of 100. At 60 units the demand curve is at US\$9 and the supply curve at US\$5. Calculate the deadweight loss.
explanation: Deadweight loss = ½ × (9 − 5) × (100 − 60) = US\$80.
hints: The deadweight loss is a triangle between the demand and supply curves from 60 to 100 units.

stem: At the competitive equilibrium, total surplus (consumer plus producer surplus) is at its maximum.
explanation: True. Every unit that is worth more to buyers than it costs to produce is traded.

stem: Tax revenue received by the government is part of the deadweight loss of a tax.
explanation: False. Revenue is a transfer to the government; only the trades that no longer take place are the deadweight loss.

stem: Match each change with its effect on total surplus.

right.content: Total surplus is at its maximum

explanation: Surplus grows with output up to equilibrium and falls when the quantity traded is below it.

stem: What name is given to the loss of total surplus when the quantity traded differs from the equilibrium quantity?
explanation: Deadweight (welfare) loss: the value of trades that no longer take place.

stem: Define producer surplus.

points.description: The difference between the price producers receive and the minimum price they would accept.
Shown as the area above the supply curve and below the price line.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Producer surplus is the difference between the price received by producers and the minimum price they would be willing to accept. On a diagram it is the area above the supply curve and below the price.

explanation: Definition and diagram.

stem: Explain why consumer surplus rises when the supply of a good increases.

points.description: Supply shifts to the right, so the equilibrium price falls.
Consumers pay less than they were willing to pay on more units.
The area between the demand curve and the lower price line is larger.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An increase in supply shifts the supply curve to the right and lowers the equilibrium price while raising the quantity. Consumers now pay less than the maximum they are willing to pay on more units, so the area between the demand curve and the price line is larger and consumer surplus rises.

explanation: Link supply shift to price, quantity and the area.
hints: Describe the cause, the price and the area.

stem: Analyse the effect of a maximum price on consumer surplus and producer surplus.

points.description: Consumers who can buy pay a lower price, which raises their surplus on those units.
Quantity traded falls because producers supply less, so some consumers cannot buy.
Producer surplus falls: lower price and lower quantity.
Total surplus falls (deadweight loss).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A maximum price below equilibrium lowers the price consumers pay, so those who can buy gain surplus on the units they obtain. However, producers supply less, so some consumers cannot buy at all and their surplus is lost. Producer surplus falls because the price and the quantity sold are lower. Overall total surplus falls because trades that benefited both sides no longer take place.

explanation: Winners, losers and the net loss.

stem: A fictional market for sacks of groundnuts has demand P = 18 − 0.1Q and supply P = 6 + 0.1Q (P in US\$ per sack, Q in sacks per week). The equilibrium is a price of US\$12 and 60 sacks. Later, new equipment lowers costs so that supply becomes P = 2 + 0.1Q and the equilibrium becomes US\$10 and 80 sacks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate consumer surplus at the original equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate producer surplus at the original equilibrium.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate consumer surplus at the new equilibrium.

points.description: Lower costs shifted supply right and lowered the price (US\$12 to US\$10).
Consumers pay less than they are willing to pay on more units (60 to 80).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Lower costs shifted supply to the right, so the price fell from US\$12 to US\$10 and quantity rose from 60 to 80 sacks. Consumers therefore gain more from each sack they buy and buy more sacks, so the area between the demand curve and the price rises.

explanation: CS 180 to 320; PS 180 at the first equilibrium.
hints: Each surplus is a triangle: half × base × height.

stem: In the groundnut market (demand P = 18 − 0.1Q, supply P = 6 + 0.1Q, price in US\$ per sack) the government sets a maximum price of US\$9 per sack. At this price the quantity demanded is 90 sacks and the quantity supplied is 30 sacks. At 30 sacks the demand curve is at US\$15 and the supply curve at US\$9.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the shortage at the maximum price, in sacks.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Assuming the 30 sacks go to the consumers who value them most, calculate consumer surplus.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why some consumers may be worse off even though the price is lower.

points.description: Only 30 sacks are supplied, so many buyers cannot obtain any.
The consumer surplus of those who go without is lost (and queues or black markets may follow).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At the maximum price producers supply only 30 sacks, far below the 90 demanded, so many consumers cannot buy at all and lose all the surplus they would have had; some may also have to queue or pay more in a black market.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** alternative way to help low-income households afford groundnuts and say why it may be better.

points.description: A targeted cash transfer or voucher to low-income households (or similar).
It leaves the price to clear the market, so there is no shortage (and less deadweight loss).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The government could give a cash transfer to low-income households. They could then afford groundnuts at the market price, so producers still supply the equilibrium quantity and there is no shortage or deadweight loss.

explanation: Shortage 60 sacks; CS 225; deadweight loss 90.
hints: Only the quantity supplied is traded.
The deadweight loss is a triangle.

stem: Assess whether a maximum price on bread makes consumers better off.

points.description: Consumers who can buy pay less and gain surplus.
Quantity supplied falls, so shortages and queues occur.
Some consumers cannot buy at all.
Black markets may charge higher prices.
Quality may fall and bakeries may close.
Low-income households may gain if they can obtain bread.
Alternatives such as cash transfers.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A maximum price below equilibrium lowers the price for consumers who can buy bread, increasing their consumer surplus. However, bakers supply less, so a shortage develops, queues form and some consumers cannot buy at all; black markets may even charge more than the old price and quality may fall. Total surplus falls. Low-income households may be better off if they obtain the bread, but the gain is uncertain and a cash transfer could help them without causing a shortage. Overall, consumers are better off only if the shortage is small and bread is allocated fairly, which is unlikely in practice.

explanation: Gains for some consumers set against shortages and the net loss.
hints: Consider winners and losers and alternatives.
